edges.relationship: Scott recalls first hearing “gender” used in a paper by Davis at the Berkshire Conferences of the 1970s (2008); her 1986 essay had quoted Davis’s call to study the significance of the sexes
edges.evidence_note: Scott's own acknowledgement, read in full in the authorised Spanish translation of "Unanswered Questions" (AHR 113:5, 2008; Debate Feminista 40, 2009, p. 101): "Ahí escuché por primera vez que se mencionaba el género; fue en una ponencia de Natalie Zemon Davis" (citing Davis 1976: 90). English renderings are atlas translations from Spanish. Scott sets her own limit on the same page: "yo no fui el origen del concepto de género, ni siquiera entre las historiadoras", and names a second, literary source in her Brown colleagues of the early 1980s. The 1986 quotation of Davis (p. 1054, n. 4) is the existing reading behind edge_1029, which records Davis's contribution to gender history as a field; this edge records Scott's acknowledged personal debt, with the 2008 recollection as new evidence. Not a claim that Davis shared Scott's later theoretical position.
edges.map_label: Davis and Scott’s first hearing of gender, 1970s–2008

edges.relationship: Scott draws on psychoanalytic theory, especially the concept of fantasy, to keep gender a critical question: gender as the relation between the normative and the psychic (2008), fantasy as a concept for feminist history (2011), and the productive incommensurability of psychoanalysis and history (2012)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read in the authorised Spanish translation of "Unanswered Questions" (2008; Debate Feminista 40, 2009, pp. 108–109): psychoanalytic theory has been useful to her, "no a sus articulaciones conservadoras"; gender is "el estudio de la relación (en torno a la sexualidad) entre lo normativo y lo psíquico, el intento de colectivizar la fantasía". Her 2012 History and Theory abstract (abstract only): psychoanalysis "can force historians to question their certainty about facts, narrative, and cause". Duke's description of The Fantasy of Feminist History (2011; publisher description): she "advocates fantasy as a useful, even necessary, concept for feminist historical analysis". In a 2018 interview she speaks of "a whole psychoanalytic dimension" in Sex and Secularism. Psychoanalysis as a body of theory is the resource; no particular Freud text is claimed. The 2008 reply explains a use of psychoanalysis that "has been useful" to her ("me ha sido útil"); it does not mark a beginning, since the 1986 essay already engaged psychoanalytic theory critically (edge_583, a separate claim about universal sexual antagonism). She still rejects "conservative" psychoanalysis.
edges.map_label: Psychoanalysis and fantasy, 2008–2012

edges.relationship: Scott argues that 1970s psychohistory, shaped by American ego-psychology, assumed a compatibility between psychoanalysis and history that undercut their critical interaction, and proposes a productive incommensurability after de Certeau (2012, in her abstract)
edges.evidence_note: Author's abstract only (History and Theory 51:1, 2012, 63–83); the article body is unread. "This was not the case with the movement for psychohistory that began in the 1970s. Then the influence of American ego-psychology on history-writing promoted the idea of compatibility between the two disciplines in ways that undercut the critical possibilities of their interaction." De Certeau supplies "theoretical insight into the uses of incommensurability"; Lyndal Roper's work shows "both its limits and its value". No strand is targeted: the abstract names American ego-psychology, not a particular psychohistorian. Moderate.
edges.map_label: Against ego-psychological psychohistory, 2012 (abstract only)

edges.relationship: French feminists caught between the abstract individual and sexual difference (Only Paradoxes to Offer, 1996), and the parity movement’s attempt to “desymbolize” sex in political representation (Parité!, 2005), as Landes and Dean read them
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: both books are unread. Landes (APSR 1997, p. 443 read) quotes Scott (p. 173): "competing feminist visions have taken one side or another of the opposition between the abstract individual (which counts women the same as men) and the individual self-defined through sexual difference (which insists on their radical unlikeness)". Dean (H-France Review 2006, read in full): the book "focuses on the challenge parité poses to French universalism" (p. 149); Scott quoted on the strategy of "desymbolization" (p. 54) and on "the human individual as plural, as a type of two" (p. 61) (Dean, p. 150); Dean's query about Muslim women and lesbians (p. 152). Scott herself links French universalism, feminist movements and the politics of the veil as objects of one question about how sexual difference is conceived (Unanswered Questions, Spanish translation, p. 108).
edges.map_label: Feminism, universalism and representation, 1996–2005

edges.relationship: The French headscarf ban read as a symptom of republican, colonial and sexual anxieties (The Politics of the Veil, 2007), and a genealogy of secularism contesting the claim that secular societies guarantee gender equality (Sex and Secularism, 2017), in her reviewers’ accounts and her own interview
edges.evidence_note: Mediated for the books, which are unread. Laborde (Books & Ideas, 2008, read in full): "Particularly acute are Scott’s analyses of the re-importation of the civilizing mission in post-colonial France"; the ban "acted as a (literally) hysterical diversion" from problems of "class, race and gender". Whitney (Literary Review of Canada, 2018, read in full): the book's "polemical aim" is "to counter the notion that gender equality is somehow inherent in secular societies", working through oppositions such as "west versus Orient, Christianity versus Islam". Scott in a 2018 interview (read in full): post-colonial studies were "critical of the notion that modernity was the end point of the civilizing process"; she sought "a critique or a genealogy that could expose these contradictions". Criticism carried here, not drawn as a separate arrow: Laborde finds the "normative premises and broader political implications" unclear, "a standard limitation of discourse analysis"; O'Grady (Times Higher Education, 2018), a philosopher, objects that the later book holds nineteenth-century Europeans to present moral standards: Scott is "anachronistic, ahistorical and oddly absolutist in demanding from 19th-century Europeans moral attitudes that tally with her own". Laborde's objection concerns normative premises and political implications; O'Grady's concerns anachronism. In the 2018 interview Scott names her own difficulty: "how do I write a critique of secularism without rejecting it". A contribution to postcolonial critique of the civilizing narrative, not membership of a school.
edges.map_label: Veil, secularism and the civilizing claim, 2007–2017

edges.relationship: Laura Lee Downs charges that Scott’s poststructuralist gender severs experience and subjectivity from the agency of the oppressed and treats discourse as “text-writ-large”; Scott replies that Downs misreads theory, which “analyzes how knowledge is produced” (1993)
edges.evidence_note: A named critic without a node, drawn from women's history, whose experience-and-agency tradition Downs defends. Downs (CSSH 35:2, 1993; p. 414 and the notes shown by the publisher read): Scott's book "has had an especially powerful impact upon historians, for it is through her eyes that many of us have become acquainted with post-structuralist thought"; "There is much to admire"; but it contains "a radical attack on the naïve suppositions of all previous feminist scholarship: a rejection of that ingenuous chain of reasoning which links subjectivity and experience to the hope that oppressed persons, too, might find some agency in history"; notes: "Scott treats discourse as text-writ-large". Scott's reply in the same issue (p. 438 read): "profound misapprehension"; "theory analyzes how knowledge is produced; theory does not produce either real life or practical politics." Distinct from Palmer (edge_920), Valverde (edge_967) and Canning (edge_702).
edges.map_label: Downs’s critique and Scott’s reply, 1993

edges.relationship: Scott answers Eley and Nield that insisting on class as the best way to analyse inequality forecloses other political categories and other ways of writing critical history (2000, in her abstract)
edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract only (ILWCH 57, 2000, 69–75); the article body is unread. Eley and Nield's essay is marked by a tension between detaching social history from "its materialist assumptions" and continuing "narratives of working-class political agency"; "By insisting that class is still the best way of analyzing inequality and mobilizing resistance to it, the authors foreclose other possibilities for thinking about contemporary politics and for writing critical history"; her questions "don't exclude class but they don't require it either". Moderate. Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay).
edges.map_label: The “class” we have lost, 2000 (abstract only)

edges.relationship: With Ethan Kleinberg and Gary Wilder, a call for “critical history” as “theorized history”, against a discipline founded on empiricism, “fetishism of archives” and a gendered dismissal of theory (Theses on Theory and History, 2018)
edges.evidence_note: The collective's own words, read in full (English booklet on the History and Theory site, 2018; cited by thesis). Prologue: theory "displaced by empires of empiricism, fetishism of archives, dictates of discipline, enforcement of orthodoxy, and impotent story-telling"; I.1: "Academic history has never managed to transcend its eighteenth century origins as an empiricist enterprise"; II.1: "An invidious distinction between a feminized philosophy and a masculinized history"; III.1: "Critical history is theorized history"; III.7: "Critical history is a history of the present". Co-authored: credit belongs to all three, and no thesis is assigned to Scott alone. A late intervention in disputes about disciplinary scrutiny, not a resolution of them.
edges.map_label: Theses on Theory and History, 2018

edges.relationship: Four questions put to White (1993): whether a determinist theory of language fits the freedom White grants historians, whether his tropology should itself be historicised, what becomes of research's “heavy and demanding operations”, and how his relativism answers the Shoah and its deniers, as White restates them in his rejoinder
edges.evidence_note: Chartier's article ("Quatre questions à Hayden White", Storia della Storiografia 24, 1993, 133–142) is unread. The four questions are known through White's 1995 rejoinder, read in full in its authorised Portuguese translation (Revista de Teoria da História 28, 2025, published 14 April 2026): (1) whether it is "contraditório" to invoke a post-Saussurean, "determinista" theory of language while granting historians a poet's freedom (p. 4); (2) whether he treated one tropology as inherent to Western consciousness instead of contextualising the historians' discourses (p. 5); (3) how to regard "opérations très lourdes et exigeantes que sont la constitution d'un corpus documentaire, le contrôle des données et des hypothèses, la construction d'interprétation" (Chartier's French, quoted by White, p. 6); (4) how White's "relativismo" meets the demand for truth raised by the "crimes commis par les tyrannies ou, plus encore, la Shoah" and by revisionist denial (pp. 7–8). Metadata of both articles from Domańska's bibliography. White calls the exchange friendly (p. 4); a critique of Metahistory's assumptions, not a rejection of White's work as a whole.
edges.map_label: Chartier’s four questions to White, 1993, as White restates them

edges.relationship: White’s rejoinder (1995): no contradiction between linguistic codes that limit what can be said and freely chosen codes; his tropology was dominant in Western discourse from the late Renaissance; much of erudition’s apparatus is a ritual “theatre” of good faith; Holocaust denial raises no methodological question
edges.evidence_note: White's own words, read in full in the authorised Portuguese translation (Revista de Teoria da História 28, 2025, e83664, published 14 April 2026; English renderings are atlas translations from Portuguese; the 1995 English original, Storia della Storiografia 27, 63–70, not seen). "Eu estava falando de discursos, não do cosmos" (p. 4); the fourfold tropology was "culturalmente dominante no Ocidente desde o final do Renascimento até o Modernismo", and "O modelo talvez tenha sido menos útil do que eu imaginava; não foi muito bem recebido. Mas era melhor, penso eu, do que não ter modelo nenhum" (p. 5); "A tradução das coisas da realidade em coisas do discurso é uma ficcionalização" and much of the operations Chartier names "pertence ao “teatro” da erudição acadêmica; tem uma função ritual" (pp. 6–7); the deniers "simplesmente (e de forma bastante perversa) negam a ocorrência de certos eventos", and "Não há qualquer questão metodológica em jogo" (pp. 7–8). A reply within a courteous exchange (p. 4), including a concession about his model's reception.
edges.map_label: White’s rejoinder to Chartier, 1995

edges.relationship: Practices are not reducible to discourse: the logic of discourses differs from the logic of conduct, social positions are conditions of possibility of discourse, and cultural historians have moved away from “the illusions of the linguistic turn” (2003)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read in full (Cahiers du CRH 31, 2003, OpenEdition; paragraphs cited). The linguistic turn holds "que la « réalité » n'est pas une référence objective, extérieure au discours"; against it, accessing past practices through texts does not mean "affirmer l'identité de deux logiques" (¶25). Social positions "ne sont pas seulement un effet des discours ; elles en désignent également les conditions de possibilité" (¶26). Cultural historians "se sont éloignés tant des illusions du tournant linguistique que des héritages contraignants qui postulaient le primat du politique ou la toute-puissance du social" (¶31). Foucault's own distinction between discursive formations and non-discursive systems is one of his resources (¶25 n. 25), so this is a critique of a position, not of every author grouped under this entry; Hayden White is not named in the article.
edges.map_label: Against reducing practice to discourse, 2003

edges.relationship: Doubts the coherence Hunt claimed for the new cultural history in 1989: by 2003 it is held together by shared questions and debate rather than by a unified approach
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read in full (Cahiers du CRH 31, 2003). He starts from Hunt's 1989 volume and its three defining traits (¶1–3) and endorses her emphasis on sexual identities as "l'un des traits originaux de la new cultural history" (¶30). Then: "La cohérence la new cultural history est-elle aussi forte que le proclamait Lynn Hunt ? La diversité des objets de recherche, des perspectives méthodologiques et des références théoriques … permet d'en douter"; the field "n'est pas, ou n'est plus, définie par l'unité de son approche, mais par l'espace d'échanges et de débats" (¶31). A bounded disagreement about one claim, within an account that adopts her categories; not a rejection of her work.
edges.map_label: Doubting a unified new cultural history, 2003

edges.relationship: Bourdieu’s distinction between practical sense and scholastic reason (cited 2003) and his account of social difference (2007 dialogue); Certeau restored the space of readers’ appropriation, though Chartier rejects reading his “poaching” as absolute freedom
edges.evidence_note: His own words. 2003 article, read in full: to think "cette irréductibilité de l'expérience au discours", historians could rely on Foucault's distinction and on "celle établie par Bourdieu entre « sens pratique » et « raison scolastique »" (¶25, n. 26: Méditations pascaliennes, 1997). 2007 dialogue with Darnton, read in part in Portuguese translation (MATRIZes 5:2, 2012): social difference "não decorre apenas dessa tradição da história social da Annales, decorre também … ao trabalho de Pierre Bourdieu" (p. 164); no contradiction between Bourdieu's sociology of cultural production and McKenzie's sociology of texts (p. 166); "De Certeau, entre outros, restituiu este espaço" between constraints and readers' appropriation, but "seria um erro acreditar que esta liberdade é absoluta" (p. 167). In 1988 he recorded five radio dialogues with Bourdieu, published as a book in 2010 (presentation, p. 162; Prismas bibliography). Named resources with qualifications, not adherence to a school.
edges.map_label: Bourdieu and Certeau: named resources, 2003–2007

edges.relationship: Later studies of the mobility of texts across attributions, printed versions, forms of publication, genres and translations: the lost Cardenio between Cervantes and Shakespeare (2011) and Éditer et traduire (2021), in their reviewers’ accounts
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: the books are unread. Boucheron's review of Cardenio (Books & Ideas, 2014; consulted through WebFetch extraction; selected quoted passages recorded; full text not collated): its problem is "the discrepancy between the mobility of texts and the stability of authorial names"; Boucheron expects the claim that the author function took its final form in the eighteenth century to "provoke debate, particularly among Medievalists": an anticipated objection, not a later controversy investigated here. Jouhaud (Prismas 26, 2022, pp. 236–237, read) quotes Éditer et traduire on "las cinco modalidades que suministran a las obras su movilidad" (attribution, printed variants, forms of publication, genres, translation). Chartier's own 2020–2021 Collège de France report (read via WebFetch extraction) describes research "vouées à comprendre les raisons de la mobilité des textes". Prismas's bibliography dates the books (2011; 2021). A contribution to the history of publishing and circulation within intellectual history; Darnton's separate strand membership is unchanged.
edges.map_label: The mobility of texts, 2011–2021, per reviewers

edges.relationship: History as “the raw material for nationalist or ethnic or fundamentalist ideologies”: national myths, anachronism and schoolbook pasts that historians must resist “as they are being formed” (1993 lecture)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read in full ("The New Threat to History", lecture opening the academic year at the Central European University, published in the NYRB, 16 December 1993; no pagination). "For history is the raw material for nationalist or ethnic or fundamentalist ideologies, as poppies are the raw material for heroin addiction … If there is no suitable past, it can always be invented"; "The most usual ideological abuse of history is based on anachronism rather than lies" (examples: Macedonia, Croatian schoolbooks, Ayodhya, Kosovo 1389); "History is not ancestral memory or collective tradition. It is what people learned from priests, schoolmasters, the writers of history books"; "We must resist the formation of national, ethnic, and other myths, as they are being formed." He also credits criticism of national myths "from within" (Israel, Ireland). The link to The Invention of Tradition (1983) rests only on the lecture's own "it can always be invented" and the existing publisher record; the 1983 introduction is unread.
edges.map_label: Against national myth-making, 1993

edges.relationship: The Age of… volumes (1962–1994) as a synthesis of “the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991”, praised by reviewers for range and analytical grasp and called “unashamedly Eurocentric” by Judt
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: the four volumes are unread. Guardian obituarists (2012, read in full): the series "distilled the history of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991" and "were not conceived as a tetralogy". Judt (NYRB 1995, read in full): the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation, now exposed to steady criticism and revision"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (his endnote 2 defends the European focus). Black (Historein 2003–4, p. 215): "authoritative and commanding overviews of international history from the 18th century to present". Anderson (LRB 2002) quotes Hobsbawm on Interesting Times as "world history shaping that experience". At the 2014 conference (Times Higher Education report) Mazower spoke of a "golden age of historical synthesis". Counterweights: Judt's Eurocentrism remark and the existing critiques by Guha and Chakrabarty (edges 979, 917).
edges.map_label: The Age of… synthesis, 1962–94, per reviewers

edges.relationship: Tony Judt: The Age of Extremes keeps the categories of the 1930s, gives Bolshevism “no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms”, devotes “just six pages” to “real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia and neglects nationalism (1995)
edges.evidence_note: A named reader without a node, drawn from political history because his charge concerns the book's political history. Judt (NYRB, 25 May 1995, read in full): the book's "defect, for there is really only one" is that "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; the claim that Sovietisation followed American intervention "is simply wrong"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject"; Hobsbawm "mostly avoids military or political narrative". Qualifications kept: Judt calls the book "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account", praises its economic analysis and calls The Age of Capital "Hobsbawm’s single greatest work". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.
edges.map_label: Judt on The Age of Extremes, 1995

edges.relationship: Industrial Britain and its workers: the standard-of-living debate of the 1950s and Industry and Empire (1968), which his readers credit with recasting the economic history of Britain
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: no economic-history text by Hobsbawm was read (his 1957 Economic History Review article is metadata only). Judt (NYRB 1995): Labouring Men, Industry and Empire and Captain Swing "substantially recast the economic history of Britain and the story of the British labor movement"; Hobsbawm is "by training and inclination an economic historian, and an analytical one at that". Guardian obituarists (2012): the "once celebrated 'standard of living' debate", in which he and R. M. Hartwell "traded arguments in successive numbers of the Economic History Review", and Industry and Empire (1968) as "a compelling summation of much of his work on Britain and the industrial revolution". Black (Historein, p. 215): "a key protagonist in the standard of living in the industrial revolution debates … something of a Cold War battleground". A pre-2000 gap repair; not a claim about the transition debate.
edges.map_label: Standard of living and Industry and Empire, per readers

edges.relationship: In Herman Paul’s 2019 assessment, White’s work became philosophy of history’s shared reference point, built on by Harlan, Kleinberg and Kuukkanen and contested by others; White himself assigned philosophy of history to the “practical past” (2010)
edges.evidence_note: Paul's author manuscript, read in full (Journal of the Philosophy of History 13, 2019; manuscript pages): "no other author occupies a position in the field that is remotely as central as White’s" (ms 1); his only measure is his own JSTOR count of History and Theory articles mentioning White (ms 10 n. 22), with Harlan, Kleinberg and Kuukkanen positioning themselves towards him (ms 10–11). White's own words, read in full (Historein 10, 2010, p. 18): "philosophy of history belongs to the class of disciplines meant to bring order and reason to a 'practical past'". Counterweight: Timmins (Reviews in History, 2011) remains "to be convinced that White's impact on historical writing is as great as the current narratives claim" — a claim about historians' practice, not philosophy of history. Reciprocal to edge_166 (the earlier philosophers White engaged), not parallel to it.
edges.map_label: Paul: White as the field’s reference point, 2019

edges.relationship: Philosophers of history contest White’s narrativism, as Herman Paul reports: Ricoeur on the constraints set by sources, David Carr on narrative in lived experience, Lorenz’s internal realism, Ankersmit on untheorised tropes and Runia on presence (1985–2013)
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: the critics' texts are unread and known through Paul's manuscript, read in full (2019, ms 17–19): Ankersmit finds the tropology "not nearly philosophical enough"; for Ricoeur sources "set constraints" and White "runs a risk of erasing genre boundaries between history and fiction" (Temps et récit 3, 1985); David Carr (1986); "'internal realists' such as Chris Lorenz argue that White downplays the importance of rational debate among historians"; Runia's "presence" against "Whitean representationalism" (2006). Paul's caveat: criticism is sometimes "a response elicited by the perceived dominance of his work" (ms 19). A second witness for David Carr: Cronon (1992, pp. 1368–1369, read) prefers Carr's position to White's and Mink's. Distinct from edge_257, where historians (Ginzburg, Evans) answer postmodernism.
edges.map_label: Ricoeur, David Carr, Lorenz, Ankersmit, Runia, per Paul

edges.relationship: A historian of European thought before Metahistory, who coauthored two textbooks on liberal humanism in Western Europe (1966, 1970) and wrote essays on the tasks of intellectual history, as Paul and Sanz Loroño report; Martin Jay ranks his reflections on the craft with Skinner’s (2013)
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: the 1960s books and essays are unread. Paul (2019, ms 13 n. 32, read in full): The Emergence of Liberal Humanism: An Intellectual History of Western Europe (1966, with Coates and Schapiro) and The Ordeal of Liberal Humanism (1970, with Coates). Sanz Loroño (Historiografías, 2011, p. 143, read in full): The Fiction of Narrative reprints "The tasks of intellectual history" and "Romanticism, historicism, and realism", the latter readable "como un Metahistory anterior al impacto del (pos) estructuralismo francés". Stovall's AHA memorial (2018, WebFetch) presents him as an intellectual historian and theorist. Jay (History and Theory, 2013, abstract only): "No contemporary intellectual historian has produced more influential reflections on the historian's craft than Hayden White and Quentin Skinner". No strand is targeted.
edges.map_label: Intellectual historian of Europe, per readers

edges.relationship: White asks what limits govern the stories that can responsibly be told about the Holocaust (Probing the Limits of Representation, 1992; reprinted in Figural Realism); the quoted excerpt makes a conditional argument about facts determining plots. His 2014 contents also list “Truth and Circumstance …”; that chapter is unread
edges.evidence_note: An excerpt witness: the passages of the essay quoted by Claus and Marriott, whose framing is theirs (white_emplotment_excerpt, existing reading, re-read for revision 1.147): "Are there any limits on the kind of story that can responsibly be told about these phenomena?"; facts set limits on stories "only if we believe that the events themselves possess a 'story' kind of form and a 'plot' kind of meaning" — a conditional argument about facts determining plots, not a claim that all emplotments are equally valid, and not the full argument of the chapter. The essay's pages (37–53 in Friedländer's volume) and its discussion by Ginzburg and Funkenstein come from Domańska's bibliography; MUSE contents show it reprinted as Figural Realism ch. 2 (pp. 27–42) and the 2014 chapter "Truth and Circumstance: What (if Anything) Can Properly Be Said about the Holocaust?" (pp. 25–40), both unread. Paul (2019, ms 15) records his later "forays into 'modernist events,' … witness literature, trauma". Holocaust representation was previously carried only at group level (edges 223, 224) and in Friedländer's roster row.
edges.map_label: Limits of emplotment, 1992 (excerpt)

edges.relationship: Cronon builds on White’s distinction between chronicle and narrative, then sides with David Carr against the White–Mink view that historians impose plots on reality (1992)
edges.evidence_note: Cronon's own text, read in part for this edge ("A Place for Stories", JAH 78:4, 1992, author-hosted copy in journal pagination): p. 1351 n. 7, "This distinction between chronicle and narrative is more fully analyzed in White, Metahistory, 5-7; White, Tropics of Discourse, 109-11"; p. 1368, White and Mink "argue that narrative is so basic to our cultural beliefs that we automatically impose it on a reality that bears little or no relation to the plots we use" (Cronon's summary of their position); n. 39 calls White's 1984 survey "useful, if biased"; pp. 1368–1369, Carr's position "gives us a way of absorbing the lessons of narrative theory without feeling we have abandoned all ties to an external reality". One essay makes both moves, so one arrow records an acknowledged and contested resource (the pattern of edge_646). edge_903 (Cronon → truthdebate) uses other pages of the same essay for his own position.
edges.map_label: Chronicle and narrative: used and contested, 1992

sources.title: Patrick Boucheron, “The Missing Play,” Books & Ideas (La Vie des idées), 10 March 2014, trans. Michael C. Behrent; review of Roger Chartier, Cardenio entre Cervantès et Shakespeare: Histoire d’une pièce perdue (Gallimard, 2011).
sources.citation: Patrick Boucheron, “The Missing Play,” Books & Ideas (La Vie des idées), 10 March 2014, trans. Michael C. Behrent; review of Roger Chartier, Cardenio entre Cervantès et Shakespeare: Histoire d’une pièce perdue (Gallimard, 2011).

verification.note: Consulted through WebFetch extraction for revision 1.147; selected quoted passages recorded; full text not collated (no pagination). The book "adopts the style and format of an investigation" and opens with the court performance of winter 1612–1613; its problem is "the discrepancy between the mobility of texts and the stability of authorial names"; Theobald's Double Falshood (1727) is examined as possibly the "only surviving textual trace"; Boucheron reports Chartier's view that the Foucauldian author function reached its "final form" in the eighteenth century and adds that "This assertion will undoubtedly provoke debate, particularly among Medievalists" (an anticipated objection); "an historical essay that is in many respects experimental". The book itself is unread.

sources.citation: Roger Chartier, « Écrit et cultures dans l’Europe moderne (2006-2016) », L’annuaire du Collège de France 121 (2024): 660–663 (report for 2020–2021).

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.147 in the journal's PDF (13 pp.): translator's presentation pp. 1–3 and the rejoinder pp. 4–13, in Portuguese; the 1995 English original was not seen, so English renderings here are translations from the Portuguese. The translation is published with the permission of the Brose-White Trust and the Hayden White Literary Estate (p. 1 n. 1). Chartier's 1993 article ("Quatre questions à Hayden White", Storia della Storiografia 24, 1993, 133–142) is unread; its questions are known only as White restates them and through the French phrases he quotes. The debate ran in Storia della Storiografia "entre 1993 e 1995" (translator, p. 2). Q1 (p. 4): whether it is "contraditório" to invoke a determinist theory of language and grant historians a poet's freedom; White: "Eu estava falando de discursos, não do cosmos." Q2 (p. 5): whether tropology should be historicised; White: the fourfold model was culturally dominant from the late Renaissance to Modernism, and "O modelo talvez tenha sido menos útil do que eu imaginava; não foi muito bem recebido." Q3 (pp. 6–7): what becomes of the "opérations très lourdes et exigeantes que sont la constitution d'un corpus documentaire, le contrôle des données et des hypothèses, la construction d'interprétation" (Chartier's French as White quotes it); White: they belong largely to the "teatro" of scholarship and have "uma função ritual". Q4 (pp. 7–8): how his relativism answers the crimes of tyrannies and "plus encore, la Shoah" and revisionist denial; White: the deniers "negam a ocorrência de certos eventos" and "Não há qualquer questão metodológica em jogo". White thanks Chartier for discussing "amigavelmente" (p. 4). Dates: the journal page assigns the translation to volume 28 (2025) and gives its publication date as 14 April 2026 (rechecked 2026-10-19); 2025 is the volume year, not an established posting date. The original rejoinder is 1995.

verification.note: Complete text read for revision 1.147 (LRB page; no pagination). The memoir is offered as the "flip side" of Age of Extremes, "not world history illustrated by the experiences of an individual, but world history shaping that experience" (Hobsbawm as quoted); "a kind of fifth volume, in more personal register, of a continuous project". On remaining in the Party after 1956 (Hobsbawm quoted): "I still belong to the tail-end of the first generation of Communists"; Anderson: "Most people would see in it evidence of an exceptional integrity and strength of character". On history: Hobsbawm gives "a good account of the rise of the analytic social history associated with the Annales and Past & Present … regretting its later retreat with the cultural turn of the 1980s" (Anderson's report); his thinking about the past is more original than Braudel's, to be seen in On History (Anderson's judgment). The memoir is unread.

verification.note: Complete text and endnotes read for revision 1.147 (NYRB page; no pagination). A "Hobsbawm generation" of historians who began between about 1959 and 1975; Primitive Rebels "first appeared in 1959"; Labouring Men, Industry and Empire and Captain Swing "substantially recast the economic history of Britain and the story of the British labor movement"; the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation"; The Age of Revolution 1962, The Age of Capital 1975 ("Hobsbawm’s single greatest work"), The Age of Empire twelve years later. verification.note: Read for revision 1.147. The Spanish translation, published with the author's permission (Debate Feminista 40, 2009, https://doi.org/10.22201/cieg.2594066xe.2009.40.1441), was read in full; pages below are Debate Feminista pages, and English renderings are the atlas's translations, not Scott's English. p. 101: at the Berkshire Conferences of the 1970s, "Ahí escuché por primera vez que se mencionaba el género; fue en una ponencia de Natalie Zemon Davis" (citing Davis 1976: 90); her colleagues at Brown in the early 1980s taught her "que las diferencias sexuales no las establecía la naturaleza, sino que esto se realizaba a través del lenguaje"; "yo no fui el origen del concepto de género, ni siquiera entre las historiadoras". p. 102: gender "trata del planteamiento de preguntas históricas; no es un tratado programático ni metodológico"; she quotes Heidi Tinsman: "lo que conforma una categoría útil para el análisis feminista es un asunto de geopolítica más que una actualización epistemológica" (Tinsman as Scott quotes her; Tinsman's article is unread). p. 108: Meyerowitz wrote that in questioning gender's continued vitality in the 1999 edition Scott moved "en direcciones nuevas"; Scott: "Eso no es totalmente correcto", and she asserts a continuing concern with "cómo se conciben las diferencias entre los sexos", whether the object is French universalism, feminist movements or the politics of the veil (Meyerowitz's article is unread). edge_678.relationship: Defends the difference between fact and fiction against “postmodernist” fashions (“We cannot invent our facts”, 1993) and reads the coauthors’ manuscript of Telling the Truth about History (1994)
edge_678.evidence_note: The 1994 acknowledgments name his detailed reading while absolving all readers of responsibility for the conclusions. This records assistance, not agreement. Revision 1.147 adds his own 1993 words, read in full ("The New Threat to History", NYRB, 16 December 1993): "postmodernist" fashions "imply that all “facts” claiming objective existence are simply intellectual constructions. In short, that there is no clear difference between fact and fiction. But there is, and for historians, even for the most militantly antipositivist ones among us, the ability to distinguish between the two is absolutely fundamental. We cannot invent our facts." The passage is brief ("I need say little about the first of these responsibilities"); the lecture's main subject is the nationalist abuse of history (see the nationaltradition critique). A contribution on the side of facts, not a critique of the 1994 coauthors.

edge_644.evidence_note: The1974 review connects Gramsci to rebellion and organization while questioning the continuing value of the organic/traditional distinction. edge_322.evidence_note: A specific contribution within a heterogeneous field. The individual and group links describe related levels of the same history, not independent evidence of several transmissions. Revision 1.147: his later histories of Marxism, How to Change the World (2011), are known through Eagleton's review (read): Hobsbawm "remains broadly committed to the Marxist camp", insists on Marx's debt to the utopians and denies that the Manifesto is deterministic. rationale: The four entries stopped at 1986 (Scott), 1989 (Chartier), 1983 (Hobsbawm) and 1973 (White) on the timeline, with one to three chronology points and none after 2000. Every new edge rests on the person's own words or a named reader's explicit statement, read in full or in part with pages; abstract-only, WebFetch-extracted, translated and metadata-only readings are labelled in the evidence notes, and unread books are attributed locally to their reviewers. No new edge repeats an existing endpoint/type combination; later work that would have duplicated an existing arrow (Scott → gender, Chartier → culture, Hobsbawm → marx) goes into roster works or an edge revision instead. Named critics without nodes are drawn through a group entry with the critic named in the text (Downs via women; Judt via political; Ricoeur, David Carr, Lorenz, Ankersmit and Runia via philhistory, as Paul reports them). Four edge revisions are made without retargeting: edge_678 and edge_322 (Hobsbawm), edge_644 (Gramsci → Hobsbawm) and edge_257 (critics → White) gain later witnesses. Retargets of Scott's older group edges, a Chartier–Darnton edge, Ginzburg and Moses arrows to White, and anything touching the capitalism debate are left out (see release/README.md).

text_revisions.old: Develops gender as a historical analysis of social relationships and power. Her 1986 formulation connects symbols, normative claims, institutions and subjectivity while insisting on historical variation.
text_revisions.new: A historian of modern France who, after studies of women’s work and the family with Louise Tilly (1975, 1978), proposed gender as a historical analysis of social relationships and power (1986), connecting symbols, normative claims, institutions and subjectivity while insisting on historical variation, and questioned experience as self-evident evidence (1991). Gender and the Politics of History (1988) made her, in Laura Lee Downs’s words, “the spokesperson for gender history”; Palmer, Valverde and Downs contested her poststructuralism. Later books, presented here through their reviewers, trace French feminists’ paradoxes between the abstract individual and sexual difference (Only Paradoxes to Offer, 1996, as Landes reads it), the parity movement (Parité!, 2005, as Dean reads it), the headscarf ban (The Politics of the Veil, 2007, as Laborde reads it) and gender in the discourse of secularism (Sex and Secularism, 2017, as Whitney and O’Grady read it); Laborde finds the veil book’s normative premises unclear, and O’Grady objects that the later book holds nineteenth-century Europeans to present moral standards. In a 2018 interview Scott asked how to write a critique of secularism without rejecting it. Answering an AHR forum on her 1986 essay (2008), she insisted that gender is useful only as a question and explained her use of psychoanalysis and fantasy to keep it critical; her reply presents the forum’s reception as geographically and politically situated, quoting Heidi Tinsman, and disputes Joanne Meyerowitz’s reading of a change of direction, asserting continuity in her concern with sexual difference. With Ethan Kleinberg and Gary Wilder she called for a theorized “critical history” (2018); Knowledge, Power, and Academic Freedom (2019), in Robin Whitaker’s account, treats academic freedom as an ethical practice and holds that disciplinary practice is no power-free zone; she has also written on the claim that history will judge (2020).

text_revisions.old: Explains how textual forms, reading practices and collective representations shape social differences. His programme joins material bibliography to differentiated appropriation, critically reworks Annales and uses conceptual resources without accepting every formulation.
text_revisions.new: A historian of reading, the book and written culture in early modern Europe who explains how textual forms, reading practices and collective representations shape social differences. His programme, set out in “Le monde comme représentation” (1989), joins material bibliography to differentiated appropriation, critically reworks Annales and uses conceptual resources without accepting every formulation. In 1993 he put four questions to Hayden White, on language, tropology, the procedures of research and relativism before the Shoah; they are known here through White’s 1995 rejoinder. In 2003 he argued that practices cannot be reduced to discourse, doubted that the new cultural history was as coherent as Lynn Hunt had claimed, and described it as a space of debate that had moved away from “the illusions of the linguistic turn”. He held the Collège de France chair “Écrit et cultures dans l’Europe moderne” from 2007 to 2016; his inaugural lecture called the tide of digital textuality a major rupture in the history of written culture, as his reviewer Christian Jouhaud quotes it. Later books, known here through their reviewers, follow the mobility of texts: the lost play Cardenio between Cervantes and Shakespeare (2011) and Éditer et traduire (2021).

text_revisions.old: Studies labour, popular protest, capitalist transformation and national identifications across different scales. Cultural evidence and explanatory synthesis coexist; his responses to criticism revise some claims while retaining others.
text_revisions.new: A historian of labour, popular protest, capitalist transformation and nations, who studies cultural evidence and explanatory synthesis across different scales; his responses to criticism revise some claims while retaining others. After Primitive Rebels (1959) and Labouring Men (1964), his four Age of… volumes (1962–1994) became, for reviewers, a synthesis of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991; Tony Judt called The Age of Capital his greatest work and criticised The Age of Extremes for keeping the political categories of the 1930s (1995). With Terence Ranger he edited The Invention of Tradition (1983); in a 1993 lecture in Budapest he told historians to resist national myths as they formed and to hold to the difference between fact and fiction. Later books include On History (1997); the memoir Interesting Times (2002), which Perry Anderson read as a fifth volume of the same project: he finds in its explanation of remaining Communist after 1956 what most readers would see as integrity, while faulting its limited engagement with the political history of European Communism and its treatment of other Marxists; How to Change the World (2011), a history of Marxism, which Terry Eagleton credits with judiciousness while criticising its handling of ideas, including Althusser, feminism and Trotskyism; and the posthumous Fractured Times (2013).

text_revisions.new: Examines how emplotment, argument and tropes organize historical accounts: narrative form helps constitute an interpretation rather than merely decorating established facts. As Herman Paul reads Metahistory (1973), it treats emplotment as one of the ways historians explain, not as a replacement for explanation. His work raises disputes about historical explanation and representation; it should not be reduced to the claim that evidence is irrelevant. He asked what limits govern responsible narratives of the Holocaust (1992, known here through quoted passages), answered Roger Chartier’s four questions about language, tropes, research and relativism (1995), and from 2010 argued, after Michael Oakeshott, for a “practical past” of memories, attitudes and values that people summon “to justify, dignify, excuse, alibi or make a case for actions” (Historein, 2010). Philosophers of history built on and contested his work: Paul (2019) calls it the field’s shared reference point, while Timmins (2011) doubts its impact on historians’ practice, and Ginzburg kept him as a target, as Perry Anderson reads Threads and Traces (2012).
